mechanism.rule: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Rubber Tire Manufacturing (2024 amendments, 40 CFR part 63, subpart XXXX, RIN 2060-AV70)
mechanism.required: The rule set emission limits for the rubber processing subcategory of the Rubber Tire Manufacturing NESHAP. It applies to rubber tire plants that are major sources of hazardous air pollutants. The category had 15 major-source facilities, and 12 of them perform rubber processing. The limits were on total hydrocarbons (THC), used as a surrogate for organic HAP, and filterable particulate matter (fPM), used as a surrogate for metal HAP. Facilities could show compliance by averaging emissions across mixers at the same facility. Existing sources had 3 years to comply (Nov. 29, 2027). EPA expected facilities to meet the limits by installing regenerative thermal oxidizers (RTOs) or similar control devices. H.J.Res. 61 as enacted: Congress disapproves the rule (89 Fed. Reg. 94886 (November 29, 2024)), and it shall have no force or effect.
mechanism.benefits: EPA's own estimates, from the final rule preamble: installing RTOs or similar devices would cut THC by 94 Mg (104 tons) across the source category. EPA also estimated a cut in metal HAP emissions of 160 lb/yr. Both are annual figures. EPA said it was unable to quantify the benefits of reducing HAPs and gave a qualitative assessment instead. EPA said it was reasonable to expect the reductions to improve air quality and public health for populations exposed to emissions from these facilities.
mechanism.costs: EPA's own estimates: total annualized cost to existing sources of $13.3 million per year. Recordkeeping and reporting costs for all facilities under the whole NESHAP were estimated at $2.12 million per year. For comparison, the 2023 proposal had estimated $20.8 million per year. I found no CBO, GAO or court finding disputing EPA's cost or benefit estimates. The sponsors say EPA quantified CO2-related 'disbenefits' of $2.7–8.1 million per year on top of the $13.3 million. That is the sponsors' characterization (Sen. Scott press release).
mechanism.agency_reasons: EPA said it was amending the Rubber Tire NESHAP as the Clean Air Act requires. The rule's stated aim was to ensure that all HAP emissions from the source category are regulated; rubber processing was the only unregulated subcategory. The rule addresses Louisiana Environmental Action Network v. EPA (D.C. Cir. 2020), which requires EPA to address unregulated emissions from a major source category when it does the 8-year technology review.
mechanism.sponsor_reasons: Rep. Morgan Griffith introduced the resolution, with Sens. Tim Scott and Roger Wicker leading in the Senate. Their press materials quote the CEO of the U.S. Tire Manufacturers Association saying that tire manufacturers already comply with stringent air emission rules, and that the revised rule creates an adverse environmental impact, imposes significant financial burdens and provides negligible, if any, benefits. The sponsors also say compliance would require RTOs, which would increase CO2 emissions. Griffith said the standard used questionable emissions data and pointed to negligible health benefits as justification.
mechanism.status: The resolution became law. H.J.Res. 61 became Public Law 119-14 on 05/23/2025. The House passed it on 2025-03-05 and the Senate passed it on 2025-05-06. The 2024 rule is void. EPA says that under the joint resolution and the CRA the 2024 rule has no legal force or effect. In a Federal Register notice published 2026-06-22, EPA removed the 2024 rule's changes to 40 CFR part 63, subpart XXXX and reverted to the regulatory text in effect under the 2020 final rule.

outcomes.claim: EPA's pre-vote forecast was that the rule would have cut THC emissions by 104 tons per year and metal HAP emissions by 160 lb per year, across 15 major-source facilities (12 with rubber processing). EPA said it could not quantify the resulting health benefits, so no figure exists for avoided illness. This is a forecast made before the vote and does not record an actual outcome.

source.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Rubber Tire Manufacturing (final rule)

outcomes.counterpoint: EPA's 2020 risk review put the cancer risk to the most-exposed individual at 4-in-1 million. EPA found that risk acceptable and the existing NESHAP protective with an ample margin of safety. The 104-ton and 160-lb figures are EPA projections of what would have happened if the rule had taken effect. Compliance was not due until about Nov. 2027.

outcomes.claim: EPA estimated the total annualized cost of the final rule to existing sources in the Rubber Tire Manufacturing source category at $13.3 million per year. It separately estimated recordkeeping and reporting costs for all facilities under the NESHAP at $2.12 million per year. These are EPA's forecasts of costs, not data on what facilities actually spent.

source.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Rubber Tire Manufacturing (final rule)

outcomes.quote: We estimate the total annualized cost of the final rule to existing sources in the Rubber Tire Manufacturing source category to be $13.3 million per year.
outcomes.counterpoint: The two figures may not be additive. The $2.12 million recordkeeping and reporting estimate includes $1.97 million per year for monitoring systems, which appear to overlap the CEMS costs in the rule's cost table. I found no CBO, GAO or court finding on the cost estimates.

outcomes.claim: The regulatory status changed in the official record. The 2024 rule ceased to have legal effect on May 23, 2025. On June 22, 2026 EPA published a final action removing its provisions from the CFR and restoring the 2020 text, under which the rubber processing affected source has no emission limitations or other requirements. Rubber-processing mixers at major sources are therefore again not subject to HAP emission standards under this NESHAP.

source.title: Congressional Review Act Revocation of 2024 Amendments to the NESHAP: Rubber Tire Manufacturing

outcomes.counterpoint: This documents a legal change only, not any change in actual emissions or health. The 2020 RTR rule remains in effect. EPA's notice allows petitions for review in the D.C. Circuit; I found no record of a challenge.
outcomes.quote: There are no emission limitations or other requirements for the rubber processing affected source.

notes: 1) I found no credible record of measured emissions, monitoring data, health outcomes, facility cost savings or investment decisions after May 2025 for the rubber-processing mixers. This is a valid finding of no documented outcomes beyond legal status. Outcomes 1 and 2 are pre-vote forecasts, graded 'estimated'. 2) I read the Federal Register preamble only in search extracts. The full regulatory impact material (capital cost table, CO2 'disbenefit' calculation, risk review for the 2024 action) was not opened. The $61M capital figure comes from Politico Pro. The 171 tons/yr combined THC+fPM figure comes from AP, LMAWMA and Politico, not directly from the preamble extract. The $2.7–8.1M disbenefit figure comes only from sponsor press releases. 3) The sponsors say EPA's risk review found the rule unnecessary for public health. EPA's 2024 stated basis was a Clean Air Act §112(d) technology-based standard following the LEAN court decision, not a risk-based finding. The two framings are not reconciled here. 4) The 2026 Federal Register notice shows an 'effective November 29, 2024' date, which appears to reflect the nullified rule's date. The CRA nullification date is May 23, 2025. 5) Congress.gov shows the resolution signed May 23, 2025. Speculum's vote record lists the Senate passage vote as 2025-05-06. 6) EPA's page gives November 13, 2024 as the signature/finalization date. Federal Register publication was Nov. 29, 2024. 7) Sponsor quotes are drawn from their press releases and news coverage, not the Congressional Record. I did not open floor statements.
